## R Markdown

This time, we will study the effect of alcohol on congenital malformations. The data are as follows.

```{r}
alc <- factor(c("0","<1","1-2","3-5",">= 6"),levels=c("0","<1","1-2","3-5",">= 6"))
alc.s <- c(0,0.5,1.5,4,7)
malf <- c(48,38,5,1,1)
no.malf <- c(17066,14464,788,126,37)
data <- data.frame(cbind(malf,no.malf,alc,alc.s))
data
```

Here, \texttt{alc} records the average number of drinks a pregnant woman has per day, \texttt{malf} the number of babies with malformations and \texttt{no.malf} the number of babies without malformations.

To study whether alcohol consumption has an effect, we can first fit a logistic model to the data with the intercept and \texttt{alc} as predictors.

```{r}
m1 <- glm(cbind(malf,no.malf)~alc,family=binomial)
summary(m1)
```

Note that the data are entered in a grouped form and that this model is saturated. This is why the deviance residuals are all zero. This is also apparent from comparing the observed counts to the fitted counts.

```{r}
m <- malf+no.malf
fitm1.malf <- predict(m1,type="response")*m
fitm1.no.malf <- m-fitm1.malf
cbind(malf,no.malf,fitm1.malf,fitm1.no.malf)
```

It is then no surprise that the odds  and odds ratios estimated using the model \texttt{m1} and the sample odds and odds ratios are the same. 

```{r}
prob.observed <- malf/(malf+no.malf)
prob.fitted <- as.numeric(predict(m1,type="response"))
a <- log(prob.observed/(1-prob.observed))
b <- log(prob.fitted/(1-prob.fitted))
exp(a)
exp(b)
exp(a)[2:5]/exp(a)[1:4]
exp(b)[2:5]/exp(b)[1:4]
```

It seems that the odds of having a malformation increase with increasing alcohol consumption of the mother. However, the effect of alcohol is not significant, as we can see from the analysis of deviance.

```{r}
anova(m1,test="Chisq")
```

Of course this does not mean that alcohol consumption as such has no effect, it simply means that the data do not provide enough evidence that the the factor predictor \texttt{alc} is significant. 

Because \texttt{alc} is ordinal (that is, its values can be ordered), we can try to turn it into a continuous predictor by assigning a score to each category. This is the variable \texttt{alc.s}

```{r}
m3 <- glm(cbind(malf,no.malf)~alc.s,family=binomial)
summary(m3)
anova(m3,test="Chi")
```
Now alcohol consumption becomes significant. Because the data are entered in a grouped form, we can test whether the fit of \texttt{m3} is adequate using the deviance.

```{r}
pchisq(deviance(m3),df=3,lower.tail=FALSE)
```
The $p$-value is high, so there is no evidence of a lack of fit. 

Alternatively, we can also merge some categories of \texttt{alc} to reduce the number of parameters.

```{r}
alc.g <- c(0,0,1,1,1)
m4 <- glm(cbind(malf,no.malf)~alc.g,family=binomial)
summary(m4)
anova(m4,test="Chisq")
pchisq(deviance(m4),df=3,lower.tail=FALSE)
```

Also here alcohol consumption becomes significant and the $p$-value of the goodness-of-fit test whether the model is adequate is high, so there is no evidence of a lack of fit either. 

To compare \texttt{m3} and \texttt{m4}, we can look at the fitted odds ratios and compare them to the odds ratios in the saturated model. 


```{r}
prob.fitted.m3 <- as.numeric(predict(m3,type="response"))
c <- log(prob.fitted.m3/(1-prob.fitted.m3))
prob.fitted.m4 <- as.numeric(predict(m4,type="response"))
d <- log(prob.fitted.m4/(1-prob.fitted.m4))
exp(c)[2:5]/exp(c)[1:4]
exp(d)[2:5]/exp(d)[1:4]
exp(b)[2:5]/exp(b)[1:4]
```

We can also compare the two models using AIC and by looking at the fitted counts and comparing them to the observed counts.

```{r}
AIC(m3)
AIC(m4)
m <- malf+no.malf
fitm3.malf <- predict(m3,type="response")*m
fitm3.no.malf <- m-fitm3.malf
fitm4.malf <- predict(m4,type="response")*m
fitm4.no.malf <- m-fitm4.malf

round(cbind(malf,fitm3.malf,fitm4.malf,no.malf,fitm3.no.malf,fitm4.no.malf),1)
```
